BOPEN.heard: Building virtual environments exam prep, key terms, walker, and the tool chain. 26 terms for getting an AI coding agent to change a Godo game and for proving that it did. With the exact term you can ask for a change that a check can decide.

BIDEA.heard: Hollow, this is Liam in for bear. Newcomers often think that when the agent says done, the change works that does not follow, done is a claim. Evidence is a check you run yourself, like a headless test that ends with exit code zero. This film goes through the terms for instructing and checking an agent, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.

BDEFS.heard: Five labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow. In the book text, the course text uses and explains the term. In the glossary, the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it. Computed, the numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs. Illustrative data, numbers chosen to show the idea not measured. Conceptual, a drawing of the idea with no data behind it.

B0101.heard: This table is the map. 26 terms in four groups, everyone about getting an agent to change a Godo game and checking that it did. The first group is the four tools. Walker, Repository, Commit and Diff, who does what and how changes are remembered.

B0102.heard: The second group is running without a window. See L.I. and Shell, flag, headless, exit code, timeout, hang, import, and cache. These terms say how a script runs the game and judges it.

B0103.heard: The third group is telling the agent, instruction file, spec, checkable instruction, permission prompt, allow rule and sandbox. These terms say what the agent knows and what it may touch.

B0104.heard: The fourth group is proving it. Claim versus evidence, regression tests, deterministic, flaky, game time, fixed frame rate, pin time step and text versus binary scene. These terms say how you know a change is real.

B0201.heard: This is the Walker Loop 6 stages in a ring with a red dot traveling round. Walker is the course's working method in its files, not a program you run. Every change goes around the same loop. Game brief, build, play, test, inspect, revise, export. For example, to add a coin to a platformer you put the coin in the brief, have the agent build it, play it, inspect what changed, revise, and only then export.

B0202.heard: The ring gives way to a line of three commits. A repository is a project folder together with its full version history. A commit is one saved snapshot in that history. For example, your platformer's folder with its scenes, scripts and art and every saved version is the repository. Saving it right after the finished flag first works with a message that says so is one commit.

B0203.heard: Each commit now shows how many lines it changed. In this made up example, 33 lines across three commits. A diff is the exact lines that change between two versions. A commit is a snapshot and a diff is the difference between two of them. It proves what changed, not that the change works. For example, after the agent raises the player's run speed in the tuning script, the diff shows one line, the old speed taken out, and the new speed put in.

B0301.heard: This is one typed command in a terminal. The program is Godot followed by its options. CLI and Shell, a CLI, a command line interface, is a program you drive by typing commands. The Shell, such as ZSH or Bash, is the program that takes the line you type and starts it. For example, instead of pressing play in the editor, you type one line that runs your platformer's test script, and the Shell hands that line to Godot.

B0302.heard: Two flags are now picked out in red. A flag is an option on one command that changes how that command runs. The headless flag turns the window off and the quit flag stops Go-Doh when it is done. The path flag carries a value, the project folder. For example, adding the import flag to a command tells Go-Doh to convert every asset of your freshly cloned platformer. Wait until it is done and then quit.

B0303.heard: On the left, a game in a window. On the right, the same run headless printing lines instead down to 25 checks, zero failures. Headless means running with no window or display at all. Physics and scripts still run but nothing is drawn. The headless flag is one flag and headless is the state it gives you. For example, the agent runs your platformer's mechanics test headless and checks the printed results without one frame shown.

B0401.heard: This is a time chart of runs against a 30 second timeout. In this made up example, the run lengths are illustrative. An exit code is the number of program hands back when it finishes. Zero means success and anything else means something went wrong. Run A finishes early with exit code zero. For example, your platformer's test script quits with zero when every check passes and with another number when any check fails. So a script knows the verdict.

B0402.heard: Two more runs appear. Run B finishes with exit code 1, a failure. Run C keeps going past the dotted line with no exit code. A hang is a run that never finishes on its own so it never returns a number and a script waiting for one waits forever. A failure finishes and tells you it went wrong. For example, a test script hits an error before it reaches its quit line and headless go-doh just sits there with no window to shut.

B0403.heard: The dotted line is now labeled, timeout 30 seconds and run C is stopped there. A timeout is a limit after which a run is stopped. A stopped run counts as a failure, never as a success. For example, you wrap your platformers headless test in a time limit, so if a broken enemy script keeps the test from ever quitting, the limit ends the run and you get a failure instead of an endless wait.

B0501.heard: Here is source picture, a file named hero.png becomes an imported copy. Import means converting a source file into the form the engine actually uses. The copy is made from version one of the source, so the two match. For example, when you save a model exported from Blender into your project, Go-Doh imports it, and the game runs on that imported copy, not on the file you exported.

B0502.heard: Now the source is edited to version 2, but the copy is still made from version 1 and the red label says stale. A cache is a stored result, reused to save time and it can go stale. Import converts a file and the cache is where that result is kept. For example, you repaint the coin sprite and until it is imported again, the copy the engine holds still shows the old coin.

B0503.heard: The copy is imported again, now made from version 2, and the label reads fresh again. Reimporting brings the cache back in line with the source. In a headless run, import first, or the engine uses whatever the cache holds. For example, after you clone your platformer onto a new laptop, you run Go-Doh once with the import flag before any test, so the cache is built from the files you actually have.

B0601.heard: This list shows six actions an agent tries, and in this made-up example, everyone asks you first. A permission prompt is a question asking you to approve one action before it happens. Six prompts out of six is safe, but you click six times and tired people click yes. For example, the agent wants to edit the player's script in your platformer, and a prompt asks whether to allow that one edit.

B0602.heard: With an allow rule for the test, three rows now run without asking, and the prompts drop to three of six. An allow rule is a saved permission that lets a command you trust run unasked. It is pre-approved and it covers only what it names. For example, you add an allow rule for the command that runs your platformers headless test so the agent can rerun it after every change, while edits to the levels still ask.

B0603.heard: Now a sandbox surrounds the project, deleting the document's folder and writing outside the project are blocked outright and one prompt is left. A sandbox is a restricted space, with walls the agent cannot cross so a mistake cannot reach the rest of the machine, and allow rule approves a command and a sandbox sets the walls. For example, an agent in a sandbox can write your game's scene files inside the project folder. But not Godo's settings folder outside it.

B0701.heard: This box holds the project rules the agent takes in first. An instruction file is a standing file of rules, such as claw.md or agents.md, so you do not repeat them every session. These rules say run headless, pin the time step, ask before changing the tuning script and report every exit code. For example, one line in your platformer's instruction file saying how to run the test stops the agent running them the wrong way.

B0702.heard: Two ways to ask for one change, a spec is a written description of what must be built. A checkable instruction is written so a check can pass or fail. Make the ball faster as vague and no check can decide it. Change speed from 160 to 192, then run the mechanics test as checkable and the run shows two of 25 checks fail. For example, a spec for your level lists two gaps, a row of spikes and a finished flag.

B0801.heard: Two balls of speed of 100 pixels per second, when drawn at 30 frames a second, one at 144. Both cover 100 pixels in a second because the code uses delta the time since the last frame. Game time is the simulation's own clock, not the wall clock. A frame is one image drawn and a second is game time. For example, a pin test can play your whole level in game time while barely a moment passes on the wall clock.

B0802.heard: The same 25 check test timed two ways, real-time 22.4 seconds, with the fixed FPS flag at 60 0.34 seconds about 66 times faster with identical results. A fixed frame rate makes every frame count as the same amount of game time without waiting for the wall clock. A pin-time step forces every simulation step to one length, for example. The agent runs your platformer's test at a fixed frame rate, so each step is the same length on any machine.

B0901.heard: This is the evidence ladder built one rung at a time from the bottom. The claim says what happened and evidence is proof that it did. Rung 1 is the agent saying done. That proves only their message exists and nothing about the game. For example, the agent reports that the coin now plays a sound when the player touches it. Until a check or a play desk shows it, that report is a claim.

B0902.heard: Rung 2 is a git diff. It proves exactly which lines changed, but not that the change works. That is a step up from a claim and still short of proof. For example, the diff shows the agent added a jump sound to the player's script, and you still do not know whether the sound plays when you jump.

B0903.heard: Rung 3 is a clean import and a check-only parse. The project loads and it scripts parse so nothing is broken in the writing of the code. It still may do the wrong thing. For example, an enemy patrols script that parses cleanly can still walk the enemy straight off the edge of its platform.

B0904.heard: Rung 4, a headless test passes with a step pinned. Three terms join. Deterministic means the same inputs always give the same result. Flaky means a test passes sometimes and fails sometimes with no change. A regression test guards a behavior that worked before. For example, the pong test that the ball reaches the ceiling is a regression test. With the step pinned, it gave the same numbers every run deterministic. In real time, it sometimes failed with nothing changed flaky. Well, at least it's a bad thing.

B0905.heard: Rung 5 you played it that proves what one person feels on one machine and nothing about other people or other machines. For example, you play your level and the jump over the second gap feels right to you while a friend on a slower laptop may still find it too hard.

B0906.heard: Rung 6, the exported build runs on the target machine. It proves the game survives packaging, the last proof on the latter, though not that anyone wants to play it. For example, you export your platformer and it starts and plays on a classmate's computer that has never had Godo installed.

B1001.heard: Two diffs of one change run speed from 160 to 192. On the left, a text scene file where the diff shows the old line and the new one. On the right, a binary file where the diff only says the files differ. Text versus binary scene. A readable scene diffs cleanly and an opaque one does not. For example, Godot saves your level as a text scene. So when the agent moves a platform, you see the one changed position line.

B1002.heard: A red line adds the regression test. A regression test guards a behavior that worked before, so after every change you run it again. If the faster run speed breaks something that used to work, a check fails. For example, in the courses Walker platformer, raising the run speed made the check that the player comes to rest when you let go of the keys fail, a behavior nobody meant to change.

B1101.heard: For look-alike pairs one at a time, claim and evidence. A claim is someone saying it works, like the word done. Evidence is a check that shows it works, like exit code zero with 25 of 25 checks passing.

B1102.heard: Commit and push. A commit saves a snapshot on your machine and it stays there. A push sends your commits to a remote repository so they reach it too. For example, you commit the new level, then push it so your teammates copy can get it.

B1103.heard: Hang in failure, a hang never finishes, and here it is still running at 60 seconds. A failure finishes with a bad exit code, here exit one, it ended and it told you.

B1104.heard: Deterministic and flaky. Deterministic means same inputs, same result, eight of eight runs alike. Flaky means the same inputs give results that vary, so some runs fail with no change at all.

B1201.heard: Each vague request becomes an exact instruction beside a chart. Check it works becomes run the headless test with the fixed FPS flag at 60 and accept only exit code 0. Done against exit code 0.25 of 25. Only the second can be checked.

B1202.heard: Make sure it does not hang becomes stop the run after 30 seconds and a timeout counts as a failure, a run that ends at 22 seconds passes. A hang is stopped at 30 seconds and fails. The timeout turns waiting into an answer.

B1203.heard: Keep the agent away from my files becomes, allow only the test command and block rights outside the project. In the chart, read, edit and run test are allowed while delete and writing outside are blocked. Three allowed, two blocked.

B1204.heard: The test is too slow becomes, pin the time step. 22.4 seconds in real time becomes 0.34 seconds, about 66 times faster.

B1205.heard: Make the player faster becomes change run speed from 160 to 192, then run the mechanics test 25 checks. Two of the 25 fail after the change. A one number change can break two checks.

B1301.heard: This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you trust an agent's change. First, did the run end with an exit code or did a timeout stop it? A stopped run is a failure, not a pass.

B1302.heard: Second was it headless with a time step pinned. A run with real time steps may not repeat the same way twice.

B1303.heard: Third, did you import first so the cache is not stale. Otherwise the engine may be running an old copy of your art or your models.

B1304.heard: Fourth is the command allowed and is everything else blocked. That means an allow rule for the test and a sandbox around the project.

B1305.heard: Fifth is the instruction checkable with a number and a test. If no check can decide it, it is still a vague request.

B1306.heard: Sixth, which rung of the evidence ladder are you standing on, then say it exactly. Not check it works, but exit code 0 with the fixed FPS flag at 60.

BVDT.heard: Let's recap, Walker is a loop and Git keeps each lap as a commit. A diff shows what changed but not that the change works. A headless run has no window so a script judges the result. A hang never ends so a timeout stops it and counts a failure. An allow rule pre-approves a command and a sandbox sets the walls. A claim says it works and evidence is a check you can run.

BHTF.heard: Quizmy on terms for working with a coding agent on a go-do game. Give me short game-making cases one at a time. Use the terms commit diff flag headless hang timeout allow rule sandbox flaky and deterministic. For each case I must name the exact term and say why it's look-alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply then tell me if I was right.

BOUT.heard: Key terms Walker and the Tool Chain at Nick Bear Brown.
